Chapter Five: The Value of Teamwork and Aggregation in Forecasting
You know, even though personal skill is important, there’s something remarkable that happens when we bring people together. The combined wisdom of a group can take forecasting to a whole new level.
We’ve all heard the saying, “two heads are better than one.” Turns out, that’s not just a nice thought—it’s backed by solid research. When people with different backgrounds and unique perspectives work together, their collective insights often outshine what any one person, no matter how talented, could do alone.
In the world of forecasting, this is usually called the wisdom of crowds. Imagine a group of independent forecasters, each making their own prediction. When you average out those predictions, you often end up with a result that's more accurate than the single best guess in the group. Why is that? Well, individual mistakes tend to balance each other out, and the shared insights help highlight the real signal.
But here’s something to pay attention to—not every group process is created equal. The real magic of aggregation depends on a few key ingredients:
First, independence. Each forecaster needs to make their estimate without getting swept up in everyone else’s opinions. If everyone just follows the crowd, you lose that crucial diversity of thought.
Next, you want diversity. A group with people from different backgrounds and ways of thinking is much more likely to spot important details that a more uniform group might miss.
And finally, decentralization. The information should flow freely without a single authority calling all the shots. This way, you get a broader mix of inputs and cut down on bias.
So, how does aggregation work in practice? There are a few common approaches.
The simplest is just simple averaging—taking everyone’s forecasts and finding the average. It sounds basic, but with a big and varied group, it’s surprisingly effective.
Sometimes, you’ll see weighted averaging, where more seasoned or accurate forecasters have a bit more influence on the final answer. This can make the results even sharper.
And then there’s deliberative discussion. Here, the group shares their reasoning and challenges each other’s assumptions before making final predictions. This back-and-forth can dig up hidden info and push the group’s collective judgment to new heights.
Let’s look at a real-world example. In forecasting tournaments, teams compete to predict global events. The teams that openly share information, debate their ideas, and combine their estimates almost always come out ahead of individuals working solo. Sure, there are plenty of disagreements and misunderstandings along the way—but that’s all part of the process. In the end, the forecasts are stronger for it.
There’s another big benefit: aggregation helps reduce the impact of individual biases. Nobody is immune to cognitive errors, but when you blend many independent predictions, one person’s mistake doesn’t throw everything off. That’s especially critical when the stakes are high and there’s no room for big errors.
So, here’s the key takeaway: while your own forecasting skills definitely matter, the best predictions often come from the teamwork and open exchange that only a group can provide. By encouraging independence, diversity, and honest communication, we can tap into the kind of collective intelligence that helps us face uncertainty with confidence.
